'''Theodore Wells Pietsch III''' (born March 6, 1945) is an American [[systematics|systematist]], [[evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]], and [[history of science|historian of science]] best known for his research on [[anglerfish]]es. He is [[professor emeritus]] in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences and curator emeritus of [[fish]]es at the [[Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture]] at the [[University of Washington]] in [[Seattle]].

Pietsch has described 72 [[species]] and 14 [[genus|genera]] of fishes and has authored or edited more than 20 books and over 270 scientific and popular articles on the relationships, [[evolution|evolutionary history]], and [[functional morphology]] of [[teleost]]s, particularly [[deep sea]] [[taxon|taxa]]. For this body of work, Pietsch was awarded the [[Robert Henry Gibbs|Robert H. Gibbs Jr.]] Memorial Award in [[ichthyology|Systematic Ichthyology]] by the [[American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists]] in 2005. His [[author citation (zoology)|zoological author abbreviation]] is Pietsch.

==Early life and education==
Pietsch was born in [[Royal Oak, Michigan]], the son of [[automotive design|automobile designer]] [[Theodore Wells Pietsch II]] and grandson of Baltimore architect [[Theodore Wells Pietsch I]]. He attended [[John Adams High School (Indiana)|John Adams High School]] in [[South Bend, Indiana]]. As a youth in the [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]], he raised [[zebrafish]] and [[earthworm]]s to sell to local [[aquarium]] and [[fishing bait|bait]] shops, which he later credited with leading him toward the [[biology|biological sciences]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://depts.washington.edu/safs/newsletter/autwin_2010-11/pietsch.html|title=SAFS Newsletter Autumn-Winter 2010-11: The Curious Case of Ted Pietsch|website=depts.washington.edu}}</ref>

Pietsch earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[zoology]] from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1967, where he initially studied [[herpetology]] under [[Arnold G. Kluge]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.burkemuseum.org/static/uwfc_history/Pietsch.htm|title=The Era of Theodore Wells Pietsch|website=www.burkemuseum.org}}</ref> On Kluge's advice, he pursued graduate study in ichthyology at the [[University of Southern California]], earning a [[Master of Science|M.S.]] in biology in 1969 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1973.<ref name="auto"/> His dissertation examined the [[osteology]] and relationships of [[ceratioidei|ceratioid]] anglerfishes of the family [[Oneirodidae]]. He first encountered [[bathypelagic zone|bathypelagic]] anglerfishes in 1967 while sorting specimens aboard a [[research vessel]] and later made the group his primary research subject.<ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.burkemuseum.org/news/love-bizarre-deep-sea-fishes|title=For the love of bizarre deep-sea fishes|website=Burke Museum}}</ref>

==Career==
After completing his doctorate, Pietsch was a [[postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellow]] at the [[Museum of Comparative Zoology]] at [[Harvard University]] from 1973 to 1975, where he worked with Karel F. Liem. He then joined the Department of Biology at [[California State University, Long Beach]], as an [[assistant professor]], teaching there from 1975 to 1978.<ref name="auto1"/>

In 1978, Pietsch was appointed assistant professor and curator of fishes at the School of Fisheries at the University of Washington. He was promoted to [[associate professor]] in 1981 and [[professor|full professor]] in 1984, and later held the Dorothy T. Gilbert Professorship in Ocean and Fishery Sciences.<ref name="auto1"/>

During his tenure, Pietsch directed [[National Science Foundation]] and [[Smithsonian Institution]] grants that rebuilt the University of Washington Fish Collection, reorganized it in a new building opened in 1990, and cataloged tens of thousands of specimens. These included major holdings of [[Pacific Ocean|North Pacific]] [[Egg#Fish eggs|fish eggs]], [[larva]]e, and [[otolith]]s transferred from the Alaska Fisheries Science Center.<ref name="auto1"/> He retired from the University of Washington in July 2015 and was named professor emeritus and curator emeritus of fishes.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web|url=https://faculty.washington.edu/twp/|title=Theodore W. Pietsch|website=faculty.washington.edu}}</ref>

In 1989, with Douglas F. Markle of [[Oregon State University]], Pietsch founded the [[Gilbert Ichthyological Society]], a regional society for [[Pacific Northwest]] ichthyologists named for well-known ichthyologist [[Charles Henry Gilbert]] (1859–1928). He served as president of the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists in 1996–1997 and hosted the society's annual meeting at the University of Washington in June 1997.<ref name="auto1"/>

==Research==
===Anglerfishes===
Pietsch is widely regarded as a leading authority on the systematics of anglerfishes. His doctoral research reduced roughly 400 previously named oneirodid species to about 130 valid taxa, and he continued revising the [[Taxonomy (biology)|classification]] of shallow-water [[frogfish]]es and deep sea ceratioids for more than five decades.<ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto1"/>

His work on [[Fish reproduction#Sexual parasitism|sexual parasitism]] in deep-sea anglerfishes has drawn broad scientific and public attention.<ref name="Pietsch 2005">{{cite journal |author=Pietsch TW |title=Dimorphism, parasitism, and sex revisited: modes of reproduction among deep-sea ceratioid anglerfishes (Teleostei: Lophiiformes) |journal=Ichthyological Research |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=207–236 |year=2005 |doi=10.1007/s10228-005-0286-2 |s2cid=24768783 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Pietsch TW, Orr JW |title=Phylogenetic Relationships of Deep-sea Anglerfishes of the Suborder Ceratioidei (Teleostei: Lophiiformes) Based on Morphology |journal=Copeia |volume=2007 |issue=1 |pages=1–34 |year=2007 | url = http://www.asihcopeiaonline.org/doi/full/10.1643/0045-8511%282007%297%5B1%3APRODAO%5D2.0.CO%3B2 |doi=10.1643/0045-8511(2007)7[1:PRODAO]2.0.CO;2|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In this [[Reproduction#Strategies|reproductive strategy]], a tiny dwarf male permanently attaches to and fuses with a much larger female. Pietsch's morphological and [[phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] analyses showed that this mode of reproduction evolved independently as many as five times within Ceratioidei. In 2020, he co-authored a study with [[Thomas Boehm (biologist)|Thomas Boehm]] and colleagues showing that ceratioid anglerfishes have lost major elements of the [[adaptive immune system]], allowing male and female [[Tissue (biology)|tissues]] to fuse without [[transplant rejection|rejection]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washington.edu/news/2020/07/30/deep-sea-anglerfishes-have-evolved-a-new-type-of-immune-system/|title=Deep-sea anglerfishes have evolved a new type of immune system |date=July 30, 2020}}</ref>

In 2009, Pietsch, Rachel J. Arnold, and David J. Hall described the [[Psychedelic Frogfish]], ''Histiophryne psychedelica'', from waters off [[Ambon Island|Ambon]], [[Indonesia]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/02/090224154912.htm|title=DNA Evidence Is In, Psychedelic Looking Bouncing Fish Is A New Species, Dubbed &apos;Psychedilica&apos;|website=ScienceDaily}}</ref><ref>"{{cite journal |vauthors=Pietsch TW, Arnold RJ, Hall DJ |title=A bizarre new species of frogfish of the genus Histiophryne (Lophiiformes: Antennariidae) from Ambon and Bali |journal= Copeia |volume= 2008 |issue= 1|pages= 37–45 |year=2008 |url= http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1643/CI-08-129 |doi=10.1643/CI-08-129|s2cid=83903760 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The species is notable for its swirling, fingerprint-like [[pigment]] pattern and hopping [[Aquatic locomotion|locomotion]]. In 2018, Pietsch served as a scientific commentator on the first recorded observation of a live [[Caulophryne jordani|fanfin seadevil]] pair, ''Caulophryne jordani'', filmed by the Rebikoff-Niggeler Foundation near the [[Azores]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washington.edu/news/2018/03/22/a-blind-date-in-the-deep-sea-first-ever-observations-of-a-living-anglerfish-a-female-with-her-tiny-mate-coupled-for-life/|title=A blind date in the deep sea: First-ever observations of a living anglerfish, a female with her tiny mate, coupled for life |date=March 22, 2018}}</ref>

===International Kuril Island Project===
From 1994 to 2000, Pietsch led the International Kuril Island Project, a National Science Foundation-funded biotic survey and inventory of the [[Kuril Islands]] conducted with the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] and [[Hokkaido University]]. Over seven summer expeditions, international teams surveyed the [[flora]] and [[fauna]] of all 30 major islands in the [[archipelago]], sampling more than 6,580 sites and collecting over 335,000 specimens.<ref name="auto1"/>

The program expanded to [[Sakhalin]] in 2001 under the name Okhotskia and produced more than 150 scientific publications.<ref name="auto1"/> Pietsch also led a two-year survey of the flora and fauna of the [[Elwha River]] Valley on [[Washington (state)|Washington state]]’s [[Olympic Peninsula]].<ref name="auto2"/>

===History of science===
Beginning in the early 1980s, Pietsch developed a parallel career as a historian of [[natural history]]. He has published books and monographs on [[Georges Cuvier]] and the 22-volume ''[[Histoire naturelle des poissons]]''; on the eighteenth-century [[bookselling|bookdealer]], [[publishing|publisher]], and [[espionage|secret agent]] Louis Renard and his ''Fishes, Crayfishes, and Crabs''; on the unpublished manuscripts and drawings of French explorer-naturalist [[Charles Plumier]]; and on the [[Indo-Pacific]] fish paintings of [[Isaac Johannes Lamotius]].<ref name="auto2"/>

Pietsch also produced annotated [[English language|English]] translations of the first four volumes of Cuvier's five-volume ''Histoire des Sciences Naturelles'', published by the [[National Museum of Natural History, France|Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle]] in [[Paris]] in 2012,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sciencepress.mnhn.fr/en/collections/archives/l-histoire-des-sciences-naturelles-de-cuvier|title=Cuvier's History of the Natural Sciences - Scientific Publications of the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris|website=sciencepress.mnhn.fr}}</ref> 2015,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sciencepress.mnhn.fr/en/collections/archives/l-histoire-des-sciences-naturelles-de-cuvier-0|title=Cuvier's History of the Natural Sciences - Scientific Publications of the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris|website=sciencepress.mnhn.fr}}</ref> 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sciencepress.mnhn.fr/en/news/museum-s-journals-switch-countinuous-stream-fast-track-publication|title=Actualité "Cuvier's History of the Natural Sciences vol.3" - Scientific Publications of the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris|website=sciencepress.mnhn.fr}}</ref> and 2023.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sciencepress.mnhn.fr/en/news/cuvier-s-history-natural-sciences-eighteenth-century|title=Actualité "Cuvier's History of the Natural Sciences the Eighteenth Century" - Scientific Publications of the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris|website=sciencepress.mnhn.fr}}</ref> The work on the fifth and final volume has been completed and accepted for publication.

In 2010, he published ''The Curious Death of Peter Artedi: A Mystery in the History of Science'', a novelized reconstruction of the 1735 drowning of Swedish ichthyologist [[Peter Artedi]] in an [[Amsterdam]] canal. The book was based on primary archival research into Artedi's relationship with [[Carl Linnaeus]]. A Swedish translation, ''Hur dog Peter Artedi?'', was published in 2023.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/anh.2025.1004|title=AILI, Hans and PIETSCH, Theodore W. Peter Artedi: reformer of 18th century zoology. Volume 1. Peter Artedi's life and works AILI, Hans and PIETSCH, Theodore W. Peter Artedi: reformer of 18th century zoology. Volume 2. Peter Artedi|first=Ingvar|last=Svanberg|date=October 19, 2025|journal=Archives of Natural History|volume=52|issue=2|pages=459–460|via=CrossRef|doi=10.3366/anh.2025.1004|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

With William D. Anderson Jr., Pietsch co-authored ''Ichthyopedia: A Biographical Dictionary of Ichthyologists'', published by the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2022. The work contains about 1,500 biographical sketches of deceased ichthyologists from [[Ancient history|antiquity]] to the twenty-first century.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.asih.org/resources/ichthyopedia-a-biographical-dictionary-of-ichthyologists|title=Ichthyopedia: A Biographical Dictionary of Ichthyologists|website=American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
Pietsch received the Robert H. Gibbs Jr. Memorial Award in Systematic Ichthyology from the American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists in 2005 for his body of systematic work on fishes. He received the ASIH Meritorious Teaching Award in Ichthyology in 2017, the Robert K. Johnson Award for Excellence in Service in 2018, and the [[Joseph S. Nelson]] Lifetime Achievement Award in Ichthyology in 2024. In 2022, the [[Society for the History of Natural History]] awarded him its Founders' Medal for his contributions to the history of natural history.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://shnh.org.uk/news/society-for-the-history-of-natural-history-2022-awards/|title=Society for the History of Natural History 2022 awards announcement. Founders' Medal - Theodore W. Pietsch; President's Award - Madeline Hutchins; Natural History Book Prize - Jordan Goodman}}</ref>

Pietsch is a fellow of the [[California Academy of Sciences]], the [[Linnean Society of London]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and the University of Washington Teaching Academy. He is also an honorary member of the Ichthyological Society of Japan, and the Russian Hydrobiological Society of the Russian Academy of Sciences.<ref name="auto2"/>

Several taxa have been named in his honor, including the [[cnidaria|coelenterate]] [[parasitism|parasite]] ''[[Hydrichthys]] pietschi''; the [[cottidae|cottid]] ''[[Icelinus]] pietschi''; the [[caristiidae|caristiid]] ''[[Platyberyx]] pietschi''; the [[myroconger|myrocongrid]] [[eel]] ''Myroconger pietschi''; the [[fossil]] [[percomorpha|percomorph]] family Pietschellidae and the genus and species ''[[Pietschellus aenigmaticus]]''; and the anglerfishes ''[[Caulophryne]] pietschi'', ''[[Kuiterichthys pietschi]]'', ''[[Oneirodes]] pietschi'', ''Oneirodes parapietschi'', and ''[[Pietschichthys]] horridus''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.washington.edu:80/burkemuseum/collections/ichthyology/people/tpietsch.php|title=Theodore W. Pietsch, Ph.D. - Ichthyology - Burke Museum|website=www.washington.edu}}</ref>
